title: Middle and passive in the present

objectives.can: Recognise present middle and passive forms and tell from the context which voice is meant.
Recognise ten common verbs that are middle in form.

explanation.summary: Greek verbs have three voices. In the active the subject acts; in the passive the subject is acted upon; in the middle the subject acts in a way that involves itself. In the present tense the middle and the passive share one set of endings, so context has to decide which is meant.

sections.heading: Three voices
body: Voice shows how the subject stands in relation to the action. In the active voice the subject does the action (ὁ Ἰησοῦς λέγει, 'Jesus says'). In the passive voice the subject receives it (ἐγείρεται, 'he is raised'). The middle voice is between the two: the subject acts, but the action comes back to it in some way, for example because it is done for the subject's own benefit, on the subject itself, or with the subject specially involved.

English has no middle voice, so a middle often has to be translated with an ordinary active verb, sometimes with 'for myself' or 'for themselves' added, and sometimes with nothing added at all. Do not expect every middle to have a neat English equivalent.

sections.heading: One set of endings
body: In the present tense the middle and the passive have exactly the same forms. The endings replace the active endings: -ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται. The connecting vowel is the same as in the active (ο before μ and ν, ε elsewhere).

The second person singular -ῃ comes from an older -εσαι. A few verbs keep a fuller form: δύνασαι ('you are able') occurs beside δύνῃ in the texts. The spelling -ῃ can also belong to a subjunctive; the mood is told by the context, and this lesson deals only with the indicative.

sections.heading: Middle or passive?
body: Because the forms are the same, you decide from the verb and the sentence. A verb that takes an agent, the person or thing that does the action, is almost certainly passive. The agent is often given by ὑπό with the genitive, as in 1 Corinthians 14:24, where someone is examined 'by all'. When no agent is given, a passive is still often meant, as in 'is sown … is raised' in 1 Corinthians 15:42–44.

If the verb is one that commonly has a reflexive or self-interested sense, such as διαμερίζονται in Mark 15:24 (the soldiers divide the clothes among themselves), a middle reading is likely. Dictionaries and grammars give the usual voice of each verb; the library's analyses record one of the two, which is a reading, not a fact printed in the spelling.

sections.heading: Verbs that are middle in form
body: A number of very common verbs have middle endings in the present but an active meaning. ἔρχομαι means 'I come' or 'I go', not 'I bring myself'; δύναμαι means 'I am able'; γίνομαι means 'I become' or 'I happen'; πορεύομαι means 'I go' or 'I travel'. They are entered in dictionaries with the -μαι ending as the headword.

Older textbooks call these verbs 'deponent', from a Latin word meaning 'to put aside', because the verb was thought to have put aside its active forms. Many grammarians now avoid that label, because the meaning of many of these verbs fits the middle voice well. This course says that the verb is 'middle in form'. For reading, it makes no difference: you recognise the ending and read the verb as active in sense.

sections.heading: Putting it together
body: When you meet a form in -εται or -ονται, first ask whether the verb is one of those that is middle in form. If it is, read it as active in sense. If not, look for an agent or for a sense of the subject being acted upon, which means passive. If the verb can be reflexive and the subject is also the beneficiary, think of the middle.

misunderstandings: Middle in form does not mean reflexive in meaning. ἔρχεται means 'he comes' and does not mean 'he brings himself'. Only some middles have a reflexive sense.
A passive form does not always have a stated agent. Many passives in the Greek Bible leave out the agent, and the reader has to supply it from the context.
The endings are not 'passive endings'. They are middle-and-passive endings, and a verb that is middle in form uses them for an active meaning.
ἔρχεται and similar forms are not passive because they end in -ται. The meaning of the verb decides, not the shape of the ending alone.

deeper.heading: Where the passive came from
body: Greek did not always keep the middle and the passive apart in form. Separate passive forms developed only in the aorist and the future, and you will meet them in later lessons. In the present and the perfect the middle and the passive stayed the same.

Its subject is the relative ὅ, standing for Ῥαββί, the word that is 'said', so the verb is passive. μένεις, by contrast, is second person singular active, from μένω.
